en.greeting: Hi! Today your voice does three jobs: it lifts your key words, it pauses on purpose so your main point lands, and it moves the stress to change what a long sentence means. The recordings are read in one calm voice, so the high words (CAPITALS) and pauses (|) are marked in the notes: say every example out loud and exaggerate a little.

steps.title: Let your voice travel
steps.text: Quick recap from B2: you correct with one strong word (TUESday, not THURSday) and present in chunks with |. Today: how far your voice travels.
steps.body:
**Pitch range** = how far your voice moves between low and high. Confident speakers **step up** high on the key word of each group, keep the small words low, and **fall** ↘ at the end of a point.
- Step up on **new information** and on **both sides of a contrast**.
- Keep **old information** low, even at the end: *'Did you like the hotel?' 'I LOVED the hotel.'* (the 'last word is strongest' rule is for new words)
- Start a new point a little higher.
The trap: Indonesian is usually spoken in a narrower, flatter range. In an English presentation, flat sounds **bored** or **unsure**.

steps.title: High words, low words
steps.text: Tap each line. The note shows the high words in CAPITALS: say them higher and a little longer, and let the rest stay low.
steps.body: In the contrast sentence, four words go high, because both sides of each contrast matter. In *I loved the hotel*, *hotel* stays low: it was already in the question.

steps.title: Which word goes up?
steps.text: Rina has just moved to a new team in Bandung.

question.prompt: Dimas asks: 'Do you like the new office?' Rina answers: 'I love the new office.' Which word does Rina raise highest?
question.explanation: *the new office* is old information: Dimas just said it, so it stays low. The new part of her answer is how she feels: *I LOVE the new office.* Raising *office* or *new* would sound as if she's comparing it with another place, or with the old office.

steps.title: Listen: Pak Hasan checks
steps.text: Pak Hasan is checking the plan for the new staff training. Press play and listen to his question.

question.listen: So the training for new staff starts at nine on Wednesday, right?
question.prompt: Listen to Pak Hasan. In fact, the training starts at ten on Wednesday. You answer: 'Almost. It starts at ten on Wednesday.' Which word do you raise highest?
question.explanation: He said **nine**; the day is right. So only *ten* steps up: *It starts at TEN on Wednesday ↘.* *Wednesday* is old information now, so it stays low even though it's the last word. Raising *Wednesday* would sound as if he got the day wrong.

steps.title: Thought groups in long sentences
steps.text: Now pauses. Long C1 sentences need you to know where one group ends.
steps.body:
A **noun phrase** (a noun plus all the words that describe it) is **one** thought group: *a significant increase in sales*. Don't pause inside it:
✗ *a significant | increase in sales over the last year*
✓ *a significant increase in sales | over the last year*
Good places: after a long subject, before a time or place phrase at the end, before *but / because / although*.
Not after every word, either: *We | saw | a | big…* sounds robotic. Aim for groups of about 3–8 words.
The trap: pausing where you run out of breath. Plan your groups and breathe at the |.

steps.title: Which reading is clear?
steps.text: Dr. Wulan is reading a news summary aloud at a policy meeting in Jakarta.

question.prompt: Dr. Wulan marks the pauses in her notes with |. Which version is chunked clearly?
options: The ministry announced a major | investment in public transport for the next five years.
The ministry announced a major investment in public transport | for the next five years.
The | ministry announced a | major investment in public | transport for the next | five years.
question.explanation: *a major investment in public transport* is one noun phrase, and *for the next five years* is a time phrase at the end, so the pause goes between them. The first version splits *a major | investment*; the third pauses in random places, as if she runs out of air.

steps.title: Pauses you choose
steps.text: Some pauses are on purpose. Tap each line; the note shows where the pause for effect goes.
steps.body:
A **pause for effect** is a little longer (about a second), used once or twice in a talk: **before** a key number or idea, so it lands high, or **after** a key point, so it sinks in.
**Why can it come after *was*?** Normally you wouldn't pause there. It works because it's clearly on purpose and followed by a strong key word. Keep the key phrase itself together (*fifty | million* ✗).
Silence, not *eee…*: silence sounds confident.

steps.title: Build up to the number
steps.text: Sari is presenting the results of a new booking system at a hospital in Surabaya.

question.prompt: Sari wants one pause for effect, just before her key figure. Which version does it best?
options: Thanks to the new system, our waiting | time is now four minutes.
Thanks to the new system, our waiting time is now | four minutes.
Thanks to the new system, our waiting time is now four | minutes.
question.explanation: The pause for effect comes right before the key figure, so the listeners wait and *FOUR minutes* lands high. *our waiting | time* splits a noun phrase, and *four | minutes* splits the number from its word.

steps.title: One sentence, seven meanings
steps.text: The classic drill. The note says which word to stress; the second sentence shows what it means.
steps.body: The stressed word is the part you're correcting, and **everything after it stays low and quick**. New since B2: **DIDN'T** = a firm denial; **THE** (said 'thee') = not *that* money. Long sentences work the same way: *I didn't say WE should close the Bandung office* = our partner should.

steps.title: Who should lower it?
steps.text: Budi is in a tense meeting about a key client in Surabaya.

question.prompt: Budi means: 'Our distributor should lower the price, not our company.' Which word does he stress in 'I didn't say we should lower the price for the Surabaya client'?
question.explanation: The part being corrected is **who** should lower the price: not *we*, but the distributor. So *WE* is strong and everything after it stays low. Stressing *I* would mean someone else said it; stressing *price* would mean we should lower something else, like the delivery fee.

steps.title: Cheat sheet
steps.text: Pitch, pauses and stress on one page, to keep next to your script before a presentation.

artifact.title: Cheat sheet · prosody for emphasis
artifact.intro: CAPITALS = high, stressed word · | = pause · || = pause for effect · ↘ = fall. These are strong tendencies, not strict laws.
rows: step up high, a little longer
Our profit grew by THIRty percent.
We've hired a new designer. She's from BAli.
stays low, even at the end
'Did you like the hotel?' 'I LOVED the hotel.'
Sales ROSE in JAKARTA but FELL in SURABAYA.
That's why we need a bigger budget. ↘
flat, narrow range; every sentence ending level or up
a whole noun phrase stays together
a significant increase in sales | over the last year
inside a group, or after every word
a significant | increase ✗ · We | saw | a ✗
before the key number or idea, once or twice
And the result? || FORty percent more customers.
FORty percent. || That's our best result ever.
stress the part you're correcting; the rest stays low
I didn't say HE took the money. (someone else did)
I DIDN'T say he took the money.
stress only the word that's different
It starts at TEN on Wednesday.
tips: One high word per group, and a fall at the end of each point: lift your hand on the key word while you practise.
Mark your script with | and ||, plan your groups, and breathe only at the marks. Silence, not eee…
Correcting someone? Stress only the part that's wrong and keep everything after it low.

steps.title: Watch and listen
steps.text: Three short extras: the seven-meanings sentence with audio, a teacher's video on thought groups, and a speech coach on confident pauses. Copy what you hear, out loud.

id.greeting: Halo! Hari ini suaramu punya tiga tugas: menaikkan kata kuncimu, berhenti dengan sengaja supaya poin utamamu mengena, dan memindahkan tekanan untuk mengubah arti kalimat yang panjang. Rekamannya dibaca dengan satu suara yang tenang, jadi kata yang tinggi (HURUF BESAR) dan jeda (|) ditandai di catatan: ucapkan setiap contoh dengan suara keras dan sedikit dilebih-lebihkan.

steps.title: Biarkan suaramu bergerak
steps.text: Ulasan singkat dari B2: kamu mengoreksi dengan satu kata yang kuat (TUESday, not THURSday) dan presentasi dalam potongan dengan |. Hari ini: seberapa jauh suaramu bergerak.
steps.body:
**Rentang nada** (pitch range) = seberapa jauh suaramu bergerak antara rendah dan tinggi. Pembicara yang percaya diri **naik** tinggi di kata kunci setiap kelompok, membiarkan kata-kata kecil tetap rendah, dan **turun** ↘ di akhir satu poin.
- Naikkan **informasi baru** dan **kedua sisi kontras**.
- Biarkan **informasi lama** rendah, walaupun di akhir: *'Did you like the hotel?' 'I LOVED the hotel.'* (aturan 'kata terakhir paling kuat' berlaku untuk kata baru)
- Mulai poin baru sedikit lebih tinggi.
Jebakannya: bahasa Indonesia biasanya diucapkan dengan rentang yang lebih sempit dan datar. Dalam presentasi berbahasa Inggris, datar terdengar **bosan** atau **tidak yakin**.

steps.title: Kata tinggi, kata rendah
steps.text: Ketuk setiap baris. Catatannya menunjukkan kata yang tinggi dengan HURUF BESAR: ucapkan lebih tinggi dan sedikit lebih panjang, dan biarkan sisanya rendah.
steps.body: Di kalimat kontras, empat kata naik, karena kedua sisi setiap kontras sama-sama penting. Dalam *I loved the hotel*, *hotel* tetap rendah: kata itu sudah ada di pertanyaan.

steps.title: Kata mana yang naik?
steps.text: Rina baru pindah ke tim baru di Bandung.

question.prompt: Dimas bertanya: 'Do you like the new office?' Rina menjawab: 'I love the new office.' Kata mana yang Rina ucapkan paling tinggi?
question.explanation: *the new office* informasi lama: Dimas baru saja menyebutnya, jadi tetap rendah. Bagian baru dari jawabannya adalah perasaannya: *I LOVE the new office.* Menaikkan *office* atau *new* terdengar seperti dia membandingkannya dengan tempat lain, atau dengan kantor yang lama.

steps.title: Dengarkan: Pak Hasan mengecek
steps.text: Pak Hasan sedang mengecek rencana pelatihan untuk staf baru. Tekan play dan dengarkan pertanyaannya.

question.listen: So the training for new staff starts at nine on Wednesday, right?
question.prompt: Dengarkan Pak Hasan. Sebenarnya pelatihannya mulai jam sepuluh hari Rabu. Kamu menjawab: 'Almost. It starts at ten on Wednesday.' Kata mana yang kamu ucapkan paling tinggi?
question.explanation: Dia bilang **nine**; harinya sudah benar. Jadi hanya *ten* yang naik: *It starts at TEN on Wednesday ↘.* *Wednesday* sekarang informasi lama, jadi tetap rendah walaupun kata terakhir. Menaikkan *Wednesday* terdengar seolah dia salah hari.

steps.title: Kelompok kata dalam kalimat panjang
steps.text: Sekarang jeda. Kalimat C1 yang panjang menuntutmu tahu di mana satu kelompok berakhir.
steps.body:
**Frasa kata benda** (kata benda plus semua kata yang menjelaskannya) adalah **satu** kelompok kata: *a significant increase in sales*. Jangan berhenti di dalamnya:
✗ *a significant | increase in sales over the last year*
✓ *a significant increase in sales | over the last year*
Tempat yang baik: setelah subjek yang panjang, sebelum keterangan waktu atau tempat di akhir, sebelum *but / because / although*.
Jangan juga setelah setiap kata: *We | saw | a | big…* terdengar seperti robot. Usahakan kelompok sekitar 3–8 kata.
Jebakannya: berhenti saat kehabisan napas. Rencanakan kelompok katamu dan ambil napas di tanda |.

steps.title: Mana yang jelas?
steps.text: Dr. Wulan membacakan ringkasan berita di sebuah rapat kebijakan di Jakarta.

question.prompt: Dr. Wulan menandai jeda di catatannya dengan |. Versi mana yang dipotong dengan jelas?
options: The ministry announced a major | investment in public transport for the next five years.
The ministry announced a major investment in public transport | for the next five years.
The | ministry announced a | major investment in public | transport for the next | five years.
question.explanation: *a major investment in public transport* adalah satu frasa kata benda, dan *for the next five years* keterangan waktu di akhir, jadi jedanya di antara keduanya. Versi pertama memecah *a major | investment*; versi ketiga berhenti di tempat acak, seolah dia kehabisan napas.

steps.title: Jeda yang kamu pilih
steps.text: Ada jeda yang disengaja. Ketuk setiap baris; catatannya menunjukkan letak jeda untuk efek.
steps.body:
**Jeda untuk efek** sedikit lebih panjang (sekitar satu detik), dipakai sekali atau dua kali dalam presentasi: **sebelum** angka atau ide kunci, supaya mendarat tinggi, atau **setelah** poin kunci, supaya meresap.
**Kenapa boleh setelah *was*?** Biasanya kamu tidak berhenti di situ. Jeda ini berhasil karena jelas disengaja dan diikuti kata kunci yang kuat. Frasa kuncinya sendiri tetap utuh (*fifty | million* ✗).
Diam, bukan *eee…*: diam terdengar percaya diri.

steps.title: Bangun menuju angkanya
steps.text: Sari sedang mempresentasikan hasil sistem pemesanan baru di sebuah rumah sakit di Surabaya.

question.prompt: Sari ingin satu jeda untuk efek, tepat sebelum angka kuncinya. Versi mana yang paling tepat?
options: Thanks to the new system, our waiting | time is now four minutes.
Thanks to the new system, our waiting time is now | four minutes.
Thanks to the new system, our waiting time is now four | minutes.
question.explanation: Jeda untuk efek datang tepat sebelum angka kunci, jadi pendengar menunggu dan *FOUR minutes* mendarat tinggi. *our waiting | time* memecah frasa kata benda, dan *four | minutes* memisahkan angka dari katanya.

steps.title: Satu kalimat, tujuh arti
steps.text: Latihan klasiknya. Catatannya menunjukkan kata yang ditekan; kalimat kedua menunjukkan artinya.
steps.body: Kata yang ditekan adalah bagian yang kamu koreksi, dan **semua kata setelahnya tetap rendah dan cepat**. Baru sejak B2: **DIDN'T** = bantahan tegas; **THE** (dibaca 'thii') = bukan uang *yang itu*. Kalimat panjang juga sama: *I didn't say WE should close the Bandung office* = mitra kita yang harus menutupnya.

steps.title: Siapa yang harus menurunkan?
steps.text: Budi sedang dalam rapat yang tegang tentang klien penting di Surabaya.

question.prompt: Maksud Budi: 'Distributor kita yang harus menurunkan harga, bukan perusahaan kita.' Kata mana yang dia tekan dalam 'I didn't say we should lower the price for the Surabaya client'?
question.explanation: Bagian yang dikoreksi adalah **siapa** yang harus menurunkan harga: bukan *we*, tapi distributornya. Jadi *WE* kuat dan semua kata setelahnya tetap rendah. Menekan *I* berarti orang lain yang bilang; menekan *price* berarti kita harus menurunkan hal lain, misalnya ongkos kirim.

steps.title: Tonton dan dengarkan
steps.text: Tiga tambahan singkat: kalimat tujuh arti dengan audio, video seorang guru tentang thought group, dan pelatih public speaking tentang jeda yang percaya diri. Tiru yang kamu dengar, dengan suara keras.
